# Permissions

Keelson only reads, on every provider. Each provider's section lists the data a scan reads and what grants it:
a token permission on Cloudflare, a team role on Vercel, IAM actions on AWS, RAM actions on Alibaba Cloud, an App permission on GitHub, a token scope and a role on GitLab, a token scope on Gitea, and for Sonar, public sources and Shodan.

## Cloudflare

The simplest token is Cloudflare's **Read all resources** template, which covers almost everything below.
Two sources need more:

- **Account API tokens** need *Account API Tokens Read*, which the template doesn't include.
- **Logpush jobs** can only be listed with a write permission, so Keelson doesn't list them; it reads Logpush health from GraphQL analytics instead.

A source the token can't read shows up under **Scans → Data coverage** with the permission it needs, and the checks that depend on it are
skipped rather than passed. Add accounts tests a token against each source before you connect it.

## Vercel

Vercel access tokens can't be limited to reading: a token can do whatever its user's role allows on each team it reaches.
Keelson only ever sends GET requests to Vercel (`test/vercel.test.ts` fails on anything else), and never asks for environment
variable values. A token created by a member with the **Viewer** role reads almost everything below; environment variable names,
the firewall configuration, drains and webhooks need a role that can see them. Create the token under **Account Settings → Tokens**,
scoped to the team you want to scan (or Full Account for every team), with an expiration date.

| Source | Who can read it | Checks that read it |
|---|---|---|
| Team settings | Any team role (Viewer or higher) | VID-001, VID-008, VDP-007, VEN-006 |
| Team members and invitations | Any team role (Viewer or higher) | VID-002, VID-003, VID-004 |
| Your access tokens | A Full Account token (a token scoped to one team can't list tokens) | VID-005, VID-006, VID-007 |
| Projects | Any team role (Viewer or higher) | VDP-001, VDP-002, VDP-003, VDP-004, VDP-005, VDP-006, VDP-008, VEN-008, VFW-002, VPL-001, VPL-002, VPL-003, VPL-004, VPL-006, VPL-005, XP-003 |
| Environment variable names and types | Developer, Member or Owner | VDP-008, VEN-001, VEN-002, VEN-003, VEN-004, VEN-005, VEN-007 |
| Project domains | Any team role (Viewer or higher) | VDP-002, VFW-002, VDM-002, XP-003 |
| Firewall configuration | Developer, Member, Security or Owner | VFW-001, VFW-002, VFW-003, VFW-004, VFW-005, VFW-006, VFW-007 |
| Domains | Any team role (Viewer or higher) | VDM-001 |
| Custom certificates | Any team role (Viewer or higher) | VDM-003 |
| Drains | Member or Owner | VMN-001, VMN-002, VMN-003, VMN-004 |
| Webhooks | Member or Owner | VMN-003 |
| Installed integrations | Any team role (Viewer or higher) | VID-009 |
| Shared environment variable names and types | Developer, Member or Owner | Supporting data for other checks |

## AWS

An access key belongs to one AWS account, so each account needs its own. In each account, create an IAM user for Keelson,
attach AWS's managed **SecurityAudit** policy, and create an access key under **IAM → Users → the user → Security credentials**.
SecurityAudit reads configuration only: it can't change anything, and it can't read the objects in your buckets or the rows in your
databases. Temporary keys (the ones that start with ASIA) aren't accepted, because they expire within hours.

Keelson signs every request itself. It sends GET requests, and to services whose APIs only accept POST (CloudTrail, KMS, ECS and
others) only the read actions listed below; the client refuses any other action before sending it, and `test/aws.test.ts` fails on
anything else. It never asks for a secret's value, never stores a policy document, and scans environment variables and start-up
scripts for credentials in memory, keeping only the variable's name and the kind found. It keeps only the last four characters of an
access key ID. To recognise DNS records that point at AWS addresses it also
reads AWS's public address-range file, without the access key.

Regional sources are read in every region enabled for the account. A region that refuses the access key (a service control policy,
for example) is skipped and shown as not readable on the Regions page: nothing there is checked or counted as passing.

| Source | IAM actions | Checks that read it |

## Alibaba Cloud

An AccessKey belongs to one Alibaba Cloud account, so each account needs its own. In each account, create a RAM user for Keelson with
**Using permanent AccessKey to access** and no console access, give it a custom policy with exactly the actions below (Add accounts
shows it ready to paste), and create an AccessKey for it. Alibaba Cloud's system **ReadOnlyAccess** policy isn't enough of a limit:
it also reads the objects in your OSS buckets and the values of your KMS secrets, which Keelson never needs. STS tokens (the ones that
start with STS.) aren't accepted, because they expire within hours, and the main account's own AccessKey is reported as a finding.

Keelson signs every request itself (Alibaba Cloud's V3 signature, and OSS's V4) and sends only GET requests. Alibaba Cloud's APIs
accept GET for changes too, so the client also refuses any action that isn't a read named in the policy before sending it, and
`test/alibaba.test.ts` fails on anything else. It never asks for a secret's value or an object in a bucket, never stores a policy
document, and scans environment variables and start-up scripts for credentials in memory, keeping only the variable's name and the
kind found. It keeps only the last four characters of an AccessKey ID.

Regional sources are read in every region ECS lists. A region that refuses the AccessKey is skipped and counted on the Resources
page, and a product the account never opened, or that a region doesn't offer, reads as empty rather than as a gap.

Keelson's policy grows when a check needs a new read. A policy made from an earlier version is a coverage gap for those reads
(the Overview names the missing actions): copy the current policy from Add accounts and replace the old one in RAM.

## GitHub

Keelson reads GitHub as a GitHub App that you register and own: it isn't tied to a person, and each organization's owners see it under
**Settings → GitHub Apps**. Register it from the pre-filled link in Add accounts, which asks for the read-only permissions below and no
webhook, then install it on the organizations to scan and paste its App ID and private key into Keelson. One App covers every
organization it's installed on; to install a private App on more than one organization, make it public under its Advanced settings.

On each scan Keelson signs a short-lived token request with the private key and asks GitHub for an installation token with read access
to the permissions below and nothing else, so even an App that was given more can only read through Keelson. That request is the one
POST Keelson sends to GitHub; every other request is GET (`test/github.test.ts` fails on anything else). Secret scanning alerts are read
without the secret's value, and only the scheme and host of webhook URLs are kept.

With **Contents**, Keelson lists each repository's files and fetches only manifest and lock files, GitHub Actions workflows and
Dockerfiles, never source code, to keep a software bill of materials with Anchore's Syft, Grype and Grant. Those three run where
Keelson runs, when installed, and aren't GitHub permissions: without one, its source below is listed as not readable.

| Source | App permission | Checks that read it |
|---|---|---|

| Organization owners | Organization permissions → Members: Read-only | GID-004 |
| Actions permissions | Organization permissions → Administration: Read-only | GAC-001, GAC-002, GAC-003 |
| Organization webhooks | Organization permissions → Webhooks: Read-only | GHK-001, GHK-002 |
| Installed GitHub Apps | Organization permissions → Administration: Read-only | GHK-004 |
| Workflow policy for fork pull requests | Organization permissions → Administration: Read-only | GAC-004 |
| Self-hosted runners and runner groups | Organization permissions → Self-hosted runners: Read-only | GAC-005 |
| Repositories | Repository permissions → Metadata: Read-only (always granted) | Supporting data for other checks |
| Code security settings | Repository permissions → Administration: Read-only | GSC-001, GSC-002, GSC-006 |
| Branch protection | Repository permissions → Administration: Read-only | GBR-001, GBR-002, GBR-004, GBR-003 |
| Rulesets that apply to default branches | Repository permissions → Metadata: Read-only (always granted) | GBR-001, GBR-002, GBR-004, GBR-003 |
| Deploy keys | Repository permissions → Administration: Read-only | GHK-003 |
| Repository webhooks | Repository permissions → Webhooks: Read-only | GHK-001, GHK-002 |
| GitHub Pages sites | Repository permissions → Pages: Read-only | GPG-001 |
| Public repositories' own self-hosted runners | Repository permissions → Administration: Read-only | GAC-005 |
| Whether public repositories publish releases | None: a public repository's releases are public | GRL-001 |
| Whether releases are immutable | Repository permissions → Administration: Read-only | GRL-001 |
| Whether Dependabot alerts are on | Repository permissions → Administration: Read-only | GSC-004, GSC-007 |
| Whether code scanning has run | Repository permissions → Code scanning alerts: Read-only | GSC-005, GSC-008 |
| Dependabot alerts | Repository permissions → Dependabot alerts: Read-only | GSC-004, GSC-006 |

## GitLab

The credential is the address you open GitLab at (https://gitlab.com, or your own instance's) and an access token with the **read_api**
scope, which reads through the API and can change nothing. A group access token of the group you scan, with the Owner role, is the best fit:
it belongs to the group, not to a person. A personal access token of one of the group's Owners works the same way. Every request is a GET to
`<your instance>/api/v4` (`test/gitlab.test.ts` fails on anything else), with the token in a header, and a redirect is never followed. A webhook
keeps the scheme and host of its address; deploy tokens keep their name, scopes and expiry (GitLab never returns their values); CI/CD
variables aren't read at all, because GitLab's API returns their values. Each project's files are listed, and only manifest and lock files,
`.gitlab-ci.yml` and Dockerfiles are fetched for its SBOM, never the code. Images in private and internal projects are listed and not
scanned: GitLab's registry takes a pull only with the token itself, which a scanner is never given. Syft, Grype, Grant and Trivy are tools
Keelson runs, when installed, and aren't token scopes. If the instance is only reachable inside your VPN, choose a network for GitLab on the
Networks page ([Networks](networks.md)).

| Source | Needs | Feeds |
|---|---|---|
| Group settings | Token scope read_api, on a token with the Owner role in the group | GLG-001, GLG-003 |
| Group members and their roles | Token scope read_api | GLG-002 |
| Group webhooks (GitLab Premium and Ultimate) | Token scope read_api, on a token with the Owner role in the group | GLH-001, GLH-002 |
| Projects, in the group and its subgroups | Token scope read_api | Supporting data for other checks |
| Protected branches | Token scope read_api, on a token with at least the Developer role | GLB-001, GLB-002, GLB-004 |
| Merge request approval rules and settings (GitLab Premium and Ultimate) | Token scope read_api, on a token with at least the Maintainer role in the project (an Owner of the group has it) | GLB-003 |
| Project webhooks | Token scope read_api, on a token with at least the Maintainer role in the project (an Owner of the group has it) | GLH-001, GLH-002 |
| Deploy keys | Token scope read_api, on a token with at least the Maintainer role in the project (an Owner of the group has it) | GLH-003 |
| Deploy tokens (never their values) | Token scope read_api, on a token with at least the Maintainer role in the project (an Owner of the group has it) | GLH-004 |
| GitLab Pages custom domains | Token scope read_api, on a token with at least the Maintainer role in the project (an Owner of the group has it) | Supporting data for other checks |
| Manifest and lock files and CI configuration, for each project's SBOM (never the code) | Token scope read_api, on a token with at least the Reporter role | GLD-001, GLD-002, GLD-003, GLD-004, GLD-005, GLD-006 |
| Software bill of materials (Anchore Syft) | Syft installed where Keelson runs: on the PATH, or its path in KEELSON_SYFT (not in the Docker image yet) | GLD-001, GLD-002, GLD-003, GLD-006 |
| Known vulnerabilities in dependencies (Anchore Grype) | Grype installed where Keelson runs: on the PATH, or its path in KEELSON_GRYPE (not in the Docker image yet). Its database, about 3 GB, is downloaded from Anchore into the data folder | GLD-001, GLD-002, GLD-003 |
| Dependency licenses (Anchore Grant) | Grant installed where Keelson runs: on the PATH, or its path in KEELSON_GRANT (not in the Docker image yet) | GLD-006 |

| Packages, vulnerabilities and stored credentials in public container images (Aqua Trivy) | Trivy installed where Keelson runs: on the PATH, or its path in KEELSON_TRIVY (not in the Docker image yet). Its database, about 1.6 GB, is downloaded into the data folder | GLM-001, GLM-002, GLM-003, GLM-004 |

## Gitea

Gitea runs on your own servers, so the credential is your instance's address and an access token from **Settings → Applications** there.
Give the token read scopes only (organization, repository and user; admin as well, on a site administrator's token, to learn who signs
in without two-factor authentication) and access to all repositories. It should belong to an owner of the organizations you scan: Gitea
shows branch rules, webhooks, deploy keys and collaborators only to someone who administers the repository. Every request is a GET to
`<your instance>/api/v1` (`test/gitea.test.ts` fails on anything else), and a redirect is never followed. A webhook keeps the scheme and
host of its address and never its secret or authorization header; a push mirror keeps the host it pushes to. If the instance is only
reachable inside your VPN, or its certificate is from your own authority, choose a network for Gitea on the Networks page
([Networks](networks.md)). Forgejo serves the same API. With the repository scope Keelson also lists each repository's files and
fetches only manifest and lock files, workflows and Dockerfiles for its SBOM, never the code; Syft, Grype and Grant are tools Keelson
runs, when installed, and aren't token scopes.

| Source | Needs | Feeds |
|---|---|---|
| Organization settings | Token scope organization: Read | Supporting data for other checks |
| Organization members | Token scope organization: Read | TEI-001, TEI-004 |
| Teams, their access and their members | Token scope organization: Read | TEI-002, TEI-003 |
| Which users sign in without two-factor authentication | Token scope admin: Read, on a token of a site administrator. Gitea tells nobody else | TEI-001 |
| Organization webhooks | Token scope organization: Read, on a token of an owner of the organization | TEH-001 |
| Repositories | Token scopes organization: Read and repository: Read, with access to all repositories (public, private and limited) | TER-001, TER-002 |
| Branch protection | Token scope repository: Read, on a token of someone who administers the repository (an owner of the organization does) | TEB-001, TEB-002, TEB-003, TEB-004 |
| Repository webhooks | Token scope repository: Read, on a token of someone who administers the repository (an owner of the organization does) | TEH-001 |
| Deploy keys | Token scope repository: Read, on a token of someone who administers the repository (an owner of the organization does) | TEH-002 |
| Collaborators outside the organization | Token scope repository: Read, on a token of someone who administers the repository (an owner of the organization does) | TEI-004 |
| Push mirrors | Token scope repository: Read, on a token of someone who administers the repository (an owner of the organization does) | TER-002 |
| Manifest and lock files, for each repository's SBOM (never the code) | Token scope repository: Read, with access to all repositories | TED-001, TED-002, TED-003, TED-004, TED-005, TED-006 |
| Software bill of materials (Anchore Syft) | Syft installed where Keelson runs: on the PATH, or its path in KEELSON_SYFT (not in the Docker image yet) | TED-001, TED-002, TED-003, TED-006 |
| Known vulnerabilities in dependencies (Anchore Grype) | Grype installed where Keelson runs: on the PATH, or its path in KEELSON_GRYPE (not in the Docker image yet). Its database, about 3 GB, is downloaded from Anchore into the data folder | TED-001, TED-002, TED-003 |
| Dependency licenses (Anchore Grant) | Grant installed where Keelson runs: on the PATH, or its path in KEELSON_GRANT (not in the Docker image yet) | TED-006 |

## Internet (Sonar)

Sonar looks at each entity from outside. It isn't a platform with an API: Keelson adds one internet account per entity, and it
starts from what the entity's other accounts know (their domains, DNS records and the addresses AWS and Alibaba Cloud hold), so it is scanned after them.
It sends nothing to the entity's own hosts. It sends the entity's domain names to crt.sh (certificate transparency logs) and to
Shodan, and its public addresses to Shodan, and looks names up in public DNS over HTTPS.

Its only credential is an optional Shodan API key, which can't change anything. Without one, Keelson asks Shodan's free InternetDB, which
gives open ports and known vulnerabilities but no products or versions, and finds hostnames from the certificate logs only. Shodan only
accepts its key in the address of each request; Keelson never puts it in an error or a log line.

| Source | What it needs | Checks that read it |
|---|---|---|
| Domains, DNS records and addresses of the entity's other accounts | None: read from their latest scans. Every account in the entity needs a scan since Sonar was added. | NDS-001, XP-012, XP-015, XP-027 |
| Certificate transparency logs (crt.sh) | None: the logs are public | NCT-001 |
| Public DNS lookups | None: public DNS over HTTPS | NCT-001 |
| What Shodan has seen on the entity's addresses | a Shodan API key for service details, or none for Shodan's free InternetDB | NSV-001, NSV-002, NSV-003, XP-012 |
| Subdomains Shodan has seen | a Shodan API key on a plan with query credits | Finding hostnames and addresses for other checks |
| Load balancers, their rules and targets, and security groups in the entity's AWS accounts | None: read from the AWS accounts' latest scans. Each needs a scan since this was added. | XP-013, XP-014, XP-015, XP-025, XP-026, XP-027 |
| Subdomains Amass found (OWASP Amass, passive) | Amass 5 installed where Keelson runs: on the PATH, or its path in KEELSON_AMASS (not in the Docker image yet) | Finding hostnames and addresses for other checks |
